plan.title: Slow down to catch up: orbital rendezvous
plan.businessGoal: Cut the phasing errors made by new mission operators of Aster Orbital Services (fictional client) in their first simulator campaign, before they assist the flight dynamics team on a satellite-servicing mission.

audience.role: New mission operators of a satellite-servicing company: engineers and technicians who will monitor rendezvous manoeuvres
audience.notes: Know speed, distance and time, and have seen a satellite orbit diagram. Have never planned an orbital manoeuvre; most expect that thrusting towards a target brings them closer.

sources.title: Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students, 4th edition, chapters 2, 6 and 7 (circular orbits, phasing manoeuvres, relative motion)
Fehse, Automated Rendezvous and Docking of Spacecraft, Cambridge University Press, 2003, chapter 3 (phasing and relative trajectories)
NASA, Gemini program mission reports: Gemini 4 (June 1965) and Gemini 6A/7 (December 1965)
AOS-FD-07, Aster Orbital Services flight dynamics handbook: phasing rules of thumb

objectives.statement: Predict how a prograde or a retrograde burn changes the altitude of the far side of the orbit, the period and the position relative to a spacecraft flying the same orbit.
objectives.criterion: Correct prediction on a rendezvous situation

objectives.statement: Calculate the burn of a phasing manoeuvre that closes a given along-track gap in a given number of orbits, with the rule of thumb Δx ≈ 3 T Δv.
objectives.criterion: Burn within 5 % of the expected value

objectives.statement: Plan a two-burn phasing manoeuvre that meets a gap, time and propellant requirement, and check it on a simulated orbit.
objectives.criterion: 3 simulated rendezvous requirements out of 3 met

items.title: Slow down to catch up
items.description: Hook: in 1965, Gemini 4 thrusted towards its rocket stage and watched it drift away; six months later Gemini 6A caught Gemini 7 from below. Goals of the module and three numbers that frame it.

lockedTexts.text: In June 1965, Gemini 4 commander Jim McDivitt tried to fly alongside the rocket stage that had just released his capsule. He pointed at it and fired his thrusters towards it. The stage drifted away: every push made the gap wider, and the crew gave up to save propellant. Six months later, Gemini 6A caught Gemini 7 by doing the opposite: it flew **below** its target, where orbits are faster, and climbed only at the end.

items.title: Lower is faster
items.description: Circular orbital speed and period as functions of the radius, with three reference orbits: the International Space Station (420 km), GPS (20,200 km) and geostationary (35,786 km).

lockedTexts.text:
In a circular orbit, gravity alone sets your speed. The closer you are to the Earth, the faster you must fly to stay in orbit, and the shorter each lap:

$$v = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{r}} \qquad T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{a^{3}}{\mu}}$$

$r$ is your distance from the centre of the Earth, $a$ the semi-major axis of the orbit (its radius, for a circle) and $\mu = 398\,600~\mathrm{km^3/s^2}$ the gravitational parameter of the Earth.

items.title: Burn backwards to move forwards
items.description: What a tangential burn does to the orbit (the far side moves, the period changes), the phasing rule of thumb Δx ≈ 3 T Δv and the second burn that stops the drift. Worked example: 1 m/s at 500 km gains about 17 km per orbit.

lockedTexts.text: A burn changes the **far side** of your orbit, not the point where you are. Burn forwards (prograde): the far side rises, each lap takes longer and you drift **behind**. Burn backwards (retrograde): the far side drops, each lap takes less time and you drift **ahead**. One orbit later you are back at the burn point, at the same altitude, but no longer at the same place along the orbit.

In a near-circular orbit of period $T$, a retrograde burn $\Delta v$ moves you ahead of a neighbour by about

$$\Delta x \approx 3\,T\,\Delta v \text{ per orbit}$$

and a prograde burn moves you back by as much. At 500 km, where $T = 5\,676$ s, 1 m/s gains about 17 km per orbit. Once the gap is closed, burn the same $\Delta v$ the other way, at the same point: you are back on the circular orbit and the drift stops.

items.title: Your turn: the first burn
items.description: Unscored practice right after the rule: the servicer flies 50 km behind the client satellite in the same circular orbit. Which first burn closes the gap? Prograde, retrograde or radial, with feedback on each.

items.title: Phasing lab
items.description: 3D simulation of a servicer and a client satellite in a 500 km circular orbit. Three requirements in a row: close a 51 km gap in one orbit; close it again with less than 2.5 m/s of propellant; let a client 34 km behind catch up within 2 orbits on the same budget. The learner chooses the first burn and the number of phasing orbits, runs the manoeuvre and reads the final gap. Scored.

questions.stem: The client satellite is **85 km ahead** of your servicer, in the same circular orbit at 500 km (period 94.6 min). You plan **two** phasing orbits. What retrograde burn must the first burn give, in m/s?

feedback.correct: Right: $\Delta v = \dfrac{\Delta x}{3\,T\,N} = \dfrac{85\,000}{3 \times 5\,676 \times 2} \approx 2.5$ m/s, retrograde. Two orbits later, at the same point, burn 2.5 m/s prograde to stop the drift.
feedback.incorrect: Start from $\Delta x \approx 3\,T\,\Delta v$ per orbit, in metres and seconds: over $N$ orbits, $\Delta v = \Delta x / (3\,T\,N)$.

misconceptions.feedback: You used $\Delta x = T\,\Delta v$. The drift per orbit is three times larger: in relative terms, a burn changes your period three times more than your speed, and the difference adds up over the whole orbit.
This burn closes 85 km in a single orbit. With two phasing orbits, each orbit only has to gain 42.5 km: divide by the number of orbits.
Write the period in seconds: 94.6 min = 5,676 s. The burn is in metres per second and the gap in metres.

questions.stem: After two phasing orbits on a lower orbit, your servicer is back at the burn point, **300 m behind** the client satellite. What do you do now?

options.text: Burn prograde by as much as the first burn
options.feedback: Right: this raises the far side back to the client's altitude. Your period is the client's again, so the drift stops 300 m behind it, ready for the final approach.

options.text: Do nothing: the gap is almost closed
options.feedback: On the lower orbit you keep gaining about $3\,T\,\Delta v$ per orbit: one orbit later you would be kilometres ahead of the client.

options.text: Burn retrograde to brake before the client
options.feedback: Braking lowers the far side even more and shortens your period: you would gain faster and overshoot the client.

spacing: D+3: two phasing calculations by email
D+10: one relative-motion plot to read
